what is dnsi.answer: DNSi uses standard DNS lookups to return short internal instructions, prepared answers, and utility results. It needs no custom DNSi client or HTTP application client on the device. Your server supplies the knowledge; AI is optional.

how do i use dnsi.answer: From a terminal: npx --package=@omodaka/dnsi dnsi-ask "your question". That asks a DNSi server over plain DNS. You can also run your own server with npm install -g @omodaka/dnsi, then dnsi-server. Any DNS tool (dig, nslookup) works too.

does dnsi need an api key.answer: You (the asker) never need a key: DNS is open, and this demo server has no AI to pay for. If someone runs a DNSi server backed by a real language model, the operator pays for that and can require a token in the question to keep strangers from spending their budget.

what is a dnsi token.answer: A per-zone password embedded in the question name (like ...t.mytoken.ask.dnsi.dev). A zone that requires a token refuses questions without the right one. It keeps abuse and cost down; it does not encrypt anything.

is this an ai.answer: This particular server is not. It answers a fixed set of prepared questions about DNSi, which is why replies are instant and cost nothing. A DNSi server can also be pointed at any AI provider; this one simply is not.

is there an ai behind this server.answer: No. This is the prepared-answers demo: a fixed set of questions about DNSi, answered without any AI. Every answer here is served from cache rules designed for it.

what tools are available.answer: Four built-in tools answer without any AI: tool.time (current UTC time), tool.uuid (random UUID), tool.echo (repeats your text), and tool.hash (SHA-256 of your text). Example: dnsi-ask --tool time, or dig TXT tool.time.ask.dnsi.dev.

what can dnsi be used for.answer: Short internal instructions and prepared knowledge for resolver-only devices, small unauthenticated utilities, terminal experiments, and controlled agent research. DNSi requires compatible DNS resolution and must be used with network authorization.

who can ask the dnsi demo server.answer: Anyone whose resolver can reach the service with compatible queries. The DNSi process rate-limits per source address and writes no per-user query logs, but recursive resolvers and network operators may log queries.

who made dnsi.answer: DNSi is an open-source experiment by @Omodaka9375. Code: github.com/Omodaka9375/DNSi - site: dnsi.dev. The npm package is @omodaka/dnsi (zero runtime dependencies, two commands: dnsi-server and dnsi-ask).

what is the time.answer: For the server's current UTC time, query the built-in time tool: npx --package=@omodaka/dnsi dnsi-ask --tool time (or dig +short TXT tool.time.ask.dnsi.dev). This is unauthenticated network data, not trusted time. Tool calls never touch an AI model.

how do i split a git commit.answer: Run git rebase -i HEAD~2, mark the commit as 'edit', then git reset HEAD^ to unstage its changes. Stage and commit the pieces separately with git add -p && git commit, then finish with git rebase --continue.

can a printer ask questions.answer: Yes. Even 20-year-old firmware has gethostbyname(). In A-record mode (qtype A), DNSi packs the UTF-8 answer into IPv4 addresses (4 bytes per address, up to 256 bytes) so any device that can resolve a hostname can read the answer.

what is a txt record.answer: A DNS TXT record carries arbitrary human- or machine-readable text inside a DNS response (up to 255 bytes per character-string, concatenated in order). DNSi uses TXT records to return full UTF-8 answers.

what is dnsi history.answer: DNS has answered 'what address is this name?' since RFC 882 in 1983. DNSi extends that pattern to general questions and deterministic micro-tools while staying inside standard DNS wire rules.

who is dnsi for.answer: Primarily embedded and infrastructure engineers serving short, non-confidential knowledge to resolver-only devices. It also supports terminal experiments and explicitly authorized agent research.
